title: Russia's Fuel Imports From India Hit Record as Refinery Strikes Redraw Crude Flows; Trump Urges Halt on Diesel Attacks
subhead: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to import a record 172,000 tonnes of oil products in August, 70 percent of it from India, even as Trump publicly urged Kyiv to stop targeting Russian diesel. Meanwhile Brent pushed toward $108 after satellite images confirmed heavy damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.

sections.heading: Russia's Record Fuel Imports From India Expose a Circular Crude Economy
sections.body:
Russia imported a record 172,000 tonnes of oil products in August, more than seven times the previous monthly record and three times its total imports for all of 2025, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), reported by Hindu BusinessLine and PTI. India supplied 70 percent of that volume, including 120,000 tonnes of gasoline worth about 78 million euros — all loaded at the Vadinar refinery, owned by EU-sanctioned Nayara Energy, in which Russia's Rosneft holds 49.13 percent. Vadinar sourced 100 percent of its crude from Russia in the first eight months of 2026, up from 81 percent for all of 2025.

As CREA put it, Russia is essentially paying a refinery it partly owns to process its own crude into fuel it can no longer produce domestically, then shipping it back halfway around the world. Each gasoline cargo was transferred between vessels in a ship-to-ship operation off Egypt before unloading at Russia's Arctic port of Beloe More, using sanctioned tankers — four of six had previously sailed under false flags. Gasoline accounted for 74 percent of Russia's August product imports, versus an average of 6 percent between 2023 and 2025.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's drone campaign has effectively erased Russia's status as a refiner-exporter, forcing Moscow into a costly, sanctions-laden re-import loop while its product export revenues hit their lowest since the 2022 invasion.

sections.heading: Trump Urges Kyiv to Stand Down on Russian Diesel Strikes
sections.body: US President Donald Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to halt strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure, blaming the attacks for driving fuel shortages, according to multiple reports including Seeking Alpha, Daily Times and MSN. The appeal came as attacks intensified on both sides and as record global diesel prices added to inflation pressure. Trump's framing ties the battlefield targeting to global fuel costs — a notable departure from Washington's earlier hands-off posture toward Ukraine's deep-strike campaign on Russian energy assets.
sections.whyItMatters: The request signals rising US pressure to treat Russian refineries as a global fuel market issue rather than purely a military target, potentially constraining Kyiv's most effective tool for draining Russian export revenues.

sections.heading: Saudi East-West Pipeline Damage Worse Than Acknowledged; Yanbu Stocks at 5-7 Days
sections.body: Satellite images released Sunday night show a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's 1,200 km East-West pipeline charred and badly damaged after Friday's drone attacks, the Guardian reported, citing Vantor imagery. The line is the world's key bypass for the Hormuz closure, carrying about 4 million barrels per day — roughly 4 percent of global supply — to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. With the pipeline down, Yanbu can sustain exports for only five to seven days, according to three industry sources, and Saudi buyers and traders warn stocks will run out unless the route restarts quickly. Sources gave conflicting repair estimates, one saying up to six weeks, another that partial pumping could resume sooner. Riyadh has not detailed the damage; it blames drones launched from Iraq. Saudi Arabia has not yet responded to queries from the Guardian and Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: The outage removes Saudi Arabia's principal escape valve from the Hormuz disruption just as Houthi advances tighten control of Bab el-Mandeb — collapsing both of the global oil system's main alternate routes simultaneously.

sections.heading: Hormuz Diplomacy Stumbles as Oman Postpones Iran-Gulf Meeting
sections.body: Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, announced late Sunday that a planned Monday meeting between Iran and Gulf Arab states was postponed 'in the interests of consensus', the Guardian, Reuters, Bloomberg and the New York Times reported. Iran had intended to present an agreement with Oman governing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which now operates under Tehran's permission-and-fee regime rather than free transit. The delay reflects disagreement among Gulf states over the terms — including Iran's push to impose service fees for passage — even as shipping through the strait remains at wartime lows and fresh attacks continue to be reported near Qeshm island.
sections.whyItMatters: The postponement dashes near-term hopes for a quick reopening of the world's most critical oil chokepoint, keeping roughly 20 percent of global seaborne crude at risk and underpinning the price spike.

sections.heading: Brent Pushes Toward $108 as Red Sea, Black Sea and Hormuz Strains Converge
sections.body: Brent crude rose more than 3.4 percent to $108 per barrel on Sunday, a level not seen since May, the Guardian reported, as the market digested the Saudi pipeline damage on top of the stalled Hormuz talks. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright warned oil markets against expecting a Hormuz breakthrough, estimating alternative transit routes are still moving only about 10 million barrels per day of crude and products, per World Oil. On the demand side, OPEC has lowered its 2026 global oil demand growth forecast, Reuters reported. Diesel prices in the US hit a record Friday, averaging above $6 a gallon. The supply crunch is compounded by separate Black Sea disruption: CREA data shows Novorossiysk crude loadings fell 58 percent month-on-month in August, with a nine-day halt — the longest since the 2022 invasion — and Russia's overall fossil-fuel export revenues fell 8 percent in August.
sections.whyItMatters: Three of the world's critical energy arteries — Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and the Black Sea export corridor — are simultaneously degraded or closed, producing a supply shock that OPEC's lowered demand outlook cannot offset near term.

sections.heading: India's Rising Role as the Arbitrage Centre of a Fractured Oil Market
sections.body: Beyond the Russian fuel trade, India is emerging as the key arbitrage node in a market where sanctions and war have scrambled normal trade routes. Moscow is increasingly reliant on Indian refiners both to process Russian crude and to supply finished products back — a pattern CREA flags as a direct consequence of the drone campaign. Indian outlets including The Hindu BusinessLine and the financial press are covering the flows closely, underscoring that the adjustment is being absorbed by a Global South energy economy rather than the traditional Atlantic trading system. India also supplied roughly 70 percent of Russia's August product imports, with South Korea adding 18,000 tonnes of gasoil and Egypt shipping 25,000 tonnes of diesel worth 16 million euros.
sections.whyItMatters: The war is entrenching a circular India-Russia energy relationship that sanctions architecture has not closed — refining Russian crude into products Russian consumers need, then shipping them back under layered circumvention.

bottomLine: For the second day running, the dominant energy story is a supply-side shock: satellite-confirmed damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline leaves Yanbu weeks from running dry, simultaneously knocking out Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass just as Oman postponed the Iran-Gulf shipping talks and Houthis tighten their grip on Bab el-Mandeb. Brent is pushing $108 and US diesel is at a record above $6 a gallon. The most consequential fresh development is on the Russia-Ukraine front: Ukrainian refinery strikes forced Moscow to import a record volume of fuel in August — 70 percent of it refined from Russian crude at an Indian plant partly owned by Rosneft — exposing how deep-strike has dismantled Russia's refining-export machine even as Trump publicly urged Kyiv to stop. That creates an unusual cross-pressure on Washington: keeping Russian diesel offline curbs Moscow's revenues but worsens the very fuel-price inflation the administration is under pressure to contain.
sources: Guardian, Reuters, Bloomberg, New York Times, Hindu BusinessLine, PTI, Financial Express, CREA, World Oil, Seeking Alpha, Daily Times, MSN, Long War Journal, Forbes
